summary: Defines the PPP Internet Protocol Control Protocol, which sets up and configures IP over a PPP link. After PPP's link is up, IPCP negotiates the IP settings for the two ends.

eli5.summary: Once two computers have connected over a line, this step lets them agree on their Internet addresses and settings so they can start sending Internet traffic.

questions: what is van jacobson header compression
what is the ppp protocol field for ip
subtitle: How two ends of a PPP link agree on IP addresses and header compression before any IP traffic flows.

tldr.problem: After a PPP link is up, each end still has to choose and configure the network-layer protocol it will carry, here IP, including which address each side uses.
tldr.mechanism: IPCP reuses the LCP packet exchange to negotiate options: IP-Address to agree on addresses and IP-Compression-Protocol to turn on Van Jacobson TCP/IP header compression.
tldr.outcome: Once IPCP reaches the Opened state, IP packets can cross the link. RFC 1332 obsoletes RFC 1172 and was later updated by RFC 3241.

today: RFC 1332 obsoletes RFC 1172 and is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 3241.

sections.title: Where IPCP Fits in PPP
sections.content:
PPP has three parts: a way to wrap datagrams for serial links, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) that sets up and tests the link, and a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs) that set up each network-layer protocol. RFC 1332 defines the NCP for IP, called the IP Control Protocol (IPCP). It also defines how to negotiate Van Jacobson TCP/IP header compression.

Each end first uses LCP to configure and test the link. Then PPP sends NCP packets to pick and configure one or more network-layer protocols. Only after that can datagrams of those protocols travel. The link stays configured until LCP or NCP packets close it, or until something outside the protocol happens, such as an inactivity timer expiring or an administrator stepping in.
sections.eli5: First the two computers check the line works. Then they agree on how to talk Internet over it. IPCP is the second step.

sections.title: How IPCP Works
sections.content:
IPCP is exactly the same as LCP, with a few exceptions. It uses the same packet exchange machinery. Exactly one IPCP packet goes in the Information field of a PPP frame whose Protocol field is hex 8021.

Only Codes 1 through 7 are used: Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject. Any other Code is treated as unrecognized and gets a Code-Reject.

IPCP packets may not be exchanged until PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase, and packets received earlier should be silently discarded. Because authentication and link quality determination may still be running, an implementation should be ready to wait before timing out on a Configure-Ack. The RFC suggests giving up only after user intervention or a configurable amount of time.
sections.eli5: IPCP asks and answers questions the same way the first step did. It just waits until the line is ready, and it is patient.

sections.title: Sending IP Datagrams
sections.content:
Before any IP packet is sent, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and IPCP must reach the Opened state. Exactly one IP packet then goes in the Information field of a PPP frame whose Protocol field is hex 0021.

The largest IP packet on the link is the same as the largest Information field of a PPP frame. Larger datagrams must be fragmented. A system that wants to avoid fragmentation and reassembly should use the TCP Maximum Segment Size option (RFC 879) and MTU discovery (RFC 1191).
sections.eli5: When the agreement is done, each IP packet goes into its own envelope. If a packet is too big for the envelope, it has to be cut into pieces.

sections.title: IPCP Configuration Options
sections.content:
IPCP uses the same option format as LCP but has its own set of options. Three option types are assigned: 1 IP-Addresses, 2 IP-Compression-Protocol and 3 IP-Address. The RFC points to the most recent Assigned Numbers RFC for current values.

IP-Addresses is deprecated. Implementation experience showed it is hard to make negotiation converge with it in every case. IP-Address replaces it and is preferred. The old option SHOULD NOT be sent if a Configure-Request containing IP-Addresses or IP-Address has been received. Support for it MAY be removed once IPCP advances to Internet Draft Standard. RFC 1172 covers backward compatibility.

IP-Address negotiates the address for the local end of the link. A sender can state the address it wants, or put all zeros to ask the peer to supply one. The peer supplies it by sending a Configure-Nak that carries a valid address. If negotiation of the remote address is needed and the peer left the option out of its request, the option SHOULD be appended to a Configure-Nak. By default, no IP address is assigned.
sections.eli5: Each side can say "I want this address" or "please pick one for me." The other side can answer with an address that works.

sections.title: Header Compression Negotiation
sections.content:
The IP-Compression-Protocol option negotiates a compression protocol; by default none is enabled. Its two-octet protocol field uses the same values as the PPP Protocol field for that protocol. The only value listed is hex 002d, Van Jacobson Compressed TCP/IP.

Van Jacobson compression (RFC 1144) shrinks TCP/IP headers to as few as three bytes. The RFC says this can be a significant improvement on slow serial lines, particularly for interactive traffic. The option announces the ability to receive compressed packets, so each end must request it separately if compression is wanted both ways.

For the Van Jacobson form, Max-Slot-Id is one less than the number of slots. A note warns that some implementations have trouble with one slot, and that the example implementation only works with 3 through 254 slots. Comp-Slot-Id is 0 if the slot identifier must not be compressed, and 1 if it may be. It must not be compressed when the PPP link level cannot tell the decompressor about a reception error.
sections.eli5: Normal envelope labels are long. Compression writes a tiny shortcut label instead, which helps most on a slow line. Each side must say it can read shortcuts.

sections.title: Compressed Packet Protocol Values
sections.content:
When compression is in use, the PPP Protocol field of each IP packet tells the receiver which form it is. Three values are defined:

  • 0021: plain IP. The packet is not TCP, or it is a fragment, or it cannot be compressed.
  • 002d: compressed TCP, where the TCP/IP headers are replaced by the compressed header.
  • 002f: uncompressed TCP, where the IP protocol field is replaced by the slot identifier.
sections.eli5: A little tag on each envelope says whether it is a plain letter, a shortcut letter, or a letter that starts a new shortcut.

sections.title: Recommended Options and Security
sections.content:
The appendix recommends two options: IP-Compression-Protocol with at least 4 slots, usually 16 slots, and IP-Address only on dial-up lines.

The Security Considerations section is a single line: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.eli5: The authors suggest a couple of sensible settings. They do not talk about safety in this memo.

fields.name: Max-Slot-Id
fields.desc: Maximum slot identifier, one less than the number of slots.

fields.name: Comp-Slot-Id
fields.desc: 0: slot identifier must not be compressed. 1: it may be.

items.label: IP-Compression-Protocol
items.desc: Negotiates a compression protocol; none by default.

items.label: IP-Address
items.desc: Negotiates the address for the local end of the link.
